title: Meet the Microbe That Hulks Out and Turns Cannibal
summary:
In the microscopic world, a newly discovered predator has a terrifying party trick: it transforms into a giant and eats its siblings. Euplotes gigatrox, a single-celled protist, normally grazes on bacteria. But when conditions are right, some cells balloon to more than twice their size and turn into cannibals, gobbling up their smaller relatives. Scientists found these shape-shifters in gunk scraped from an aquarium filter in Curaçao, a Dutch territory in the Caribbean.

The transformation happens in stages, explains Ben Larson, a cell biologist at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. First, a cell develops an enlarged mouth. Then it starts dashing around erratically. Once it manages to capture a sibling, its entire body plan changes, and it grows into an "enormous cannibalistic supergiant." Regular cells walk and swim, but giants can only walk in circles. Remarkably, the giants can revert to normal size through lopsided cell division. A normal cell divides once daily, but a shrinking giant can produce up to 16 offspring in five days.

Up to 42 percent of the species' genes are involved in this size-shifting. Understanding how a single cell can switch between such different behaviors may illuminate how simple life forms develop complex traits—and perhaps how multicellular life first evolved. It's a microscopic Jekyll-and-Hyde story with big implications.
why_it_matters: This discovery matters because it shows that even a single cell can switch between radically different lifestyles without changing its DNA. Understanding that flexibility could reveal how complex behaviors and multicellular cooperation first evolved, which has implications for biology broadly.

background_read: Protists are a huge and varied group of mostly single-celled organisms; they are eukaryotes, meaning their cells contain a nucleus, but they are not animals, plants, or fungi.
The genus Euplotes is part of a subgroup called ciliates, which move and feed using tiny hair-like structures called cilia.

Curaçao, where the microbes were found, is an island in the southern Caribbean and a constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands; its waters and aquariums can harbor unusual microbial communities.
Ben Larson, the cell biologist quoted in the article, works at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, a private research university in Troy, New York.

The idea that a single cell can switch between ordinary grazing and a giant cannibal form connects to a long-standing scientific puzzle: how did cooperative multicellular life emerge from single-celled ancestors?

perspectives.description: For evolutionary biologists, Euplotes gigatrox is a promising model system. Its dramatic, reversible size change offers a rare chance to study how organisms can switch between solitary and aggressive forms, potentially shedding light on ancient transitions.

Some microbiologists may caution that aquarium gunk is an artificial environment, so the cannibalistic behavior could be a stress response or laboratory artifact. More work is needed to know how often this occurs in nature and whether it truly represents an evolutionary step.

From an ecological viewpoint, the giant cells occupy a different niche than their smaller siblings, exploiting a sudden food source. The involvement of up to 42 percent of genes suggests that size-shifting is not a simple on/off switch but a broad reorganization of cellular machinery.

If researchers identify the genetic controls behind the size shift, the findings could inform studies of cell growth and division in other organisms. The work also illustrates how curiosity about an aquarium filter can open a window into the deep history of life.
